passage:
The visitors' room at the girls' hostel smelled of phenyl and canteen tea. Papa sat stiffly on a plastic chair; Tejas, her younger brother, pretended to scroll his phone.
"So you've decided," Papa said. "No MBA."
Mehak had practised this in the bathroom mirror for a week. She held her cup with both hands. "Papa, I know you want the best for me, and I'm grateful, truly, for every fee and every sacrifice. I'm taking the field job with the water project in Rajasthan. I'd really like your blessing. But I'll take responsibility for this either way."
Papa looked out of the window for a long time. Tejas stopped scrolling.
Finally Papa said, gruffly, "Rajasthan is hot in May. Take the good water bottle."
It wasn't a yes. But it wasn't a no, and he patted her hand as he stood up.

qa.q: Where is the field job Mehak is taking?
qa.a: With the water project in Rajasthan.

qa.q: How was Mehak feeling as she held her cup with both hands?
qa.a: She was nervous but resolved, having practised for a week, wanting her father's blessing while ready to stand by her choice.

qa.q: Why did Mehak's way of speaking help Papa hear her?
qa.a: She joined real gratitude with a calm, clear decision and took responsibility, so it sounded like respect rather than rebellion.

qa.q: What might Papa be feeling when he talks about the heat and the water bottle?
qa.a: Papa seems worried and not fully ready to agree, but the practical advice and the pat on her hand show a caring, softening acceptance.

grounding: Shows a young woman stating her chosen path with both gratitude and firmness, asking for her father's blessing but taking responsibility either way.

passage:
Tuesday
Something shifted today and I want to write it down before I forget how it felt. Papa called about the second-hand bike I'm thinking of buying. Old Papa would have said, "No. Dangerous. Finished." Today he said, "It's your decision, Sahil. If you want, I'll tell you what I'd check." He listed three things, the brakes, a proper helmet, the seller's papers, and stopped. He didn't repeat them five times.
When I told him I'd also switched my elective to urban planning, he paused and said, "Not what I'd have picked. But you've thought it through, I can hear that."
Keerthana was in the café with me and saw my face. "What happened?"
"I think my dad just started talking to me like an adult."
Later he sent a message: "Proud of how you think things through." I read it four times.

qa.q: What three things did Papa say he would check?
qa.a: The brakes, a proper helmet and the seller's papers.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel reading Papa's message four times?
qa.a: Sahil felt moved and proud, surprised and delighted to be spoken to as an adult.

qa.q: What did Papa do differently that marks his new role?
qa.a: He left the decision to Sahil, offered his view once without repeating it, and accepted a choice he wouldn't have made himself.

qa.q: What might Papa be experiencing as he steps back from deciding?
qa.a: Papa may still feel some worry about the bike and the elective, but also real pride, as he learns to trust Sahil's thinking.

grounding: Shows a parent moving from decision-maker to advisor, accepting a young adult's choices and growing proud of that independence.

subtype: Stage 1: A new claim on attention [Actor]
passage: In the kitchen of their Cape Town flat, baby Emil sat on Mama's lap, shaking a shiny red rattle that jingled. Everyone smiled at him. Thabo, who was five, stood by the table holding his drawing of a lion. Nobody looked at it. He watched Emil for a long time. Then he walked over, grabbed the rattle and threw it on the floor. Emil wailed. Mama said, "Thabo!" Thabo's lip wobbled. A minute later he patted Emil's foot, very gently, and then hid behind the curtain.

qa.q: What was Thabo holding while he stood by the table?
qa.a: His drawing of a lion.

qa.q: Why did Thabo grab the rattle?
qa.a: He felt left out and hurt that nobody looked at his lion drawing, and since he could not say it, it came out as grabbing.

qa.q: What could Mama do next to help Thabo?
qa.a: After settling Emil, she could look at Thabo's lion and say something like, 'It's hard when the baby gets all the looks,' so his feeling has words.

qa.q: What is it like for Emil when the rattle is grabbed?
qa.a: Emil is startled and upset, wailing when his shiny toy is suddenly snatched and thrown.

grounding: Shows a five-year-old who loves and resents his baby brother, his hurt coming out as grabbing because he cannot put it into words.

passage: Note for Mr and Mrs Menon, from the afternoon sitter, Thursday. At four, I was helping Rekha build a block tower on the rug. Akash, colouring at the table, called out twice, "Look at mine!" Each time I said, "In a minute." Then he swept the tower down and turned straight to look at me, not at Rekha. Rekha cried. When I asked why, Akash shrugged: "I don't know." I think any look felt better than none. I comforted Rekha, then sat with Akash and properly admired his colouring. He calmed at once. Perhaps he needs a little one-to-one time around four.

qa.q: What did Akash call out twice from the table?
qa.a: He called out, "Look at mine!"

qa.q: What did Akash want when he looked at the sitter after knocking down the tower?
qa.a: He felt left out and wanted attention; even a cross look felt better than being ignored.

qa.q: What small change could prevent the next knocked-down tower?
qa.a: Giving Akash a little one-to-one time around four, and looking at his work when he asks, before he feels invisible.

qa.q: What is it like for Rekha when her tower is swept down?
qa.a: Rekha is shocked and upset, crying as her careful tower falls for no reason she can see.

grounding: Shows a young child knocking over his sister's blocks to win a grown-up's attention, even a cross one, without knowing why he did it.

passage:
Monday. Jeevan pushed Irawati's doll off the sofa. Irawati screamed and hit his arm. "He started!" "She hit me!" Both cried until Amma came.
Wednesday. Jeevan took Irawati's crayon. She hit him first this time, and he hit back. "She started!" "He took it!" Irawati's face went red and wet. Nobody remembered the crayon.
Saturday. Jeevan only looked at her tower. Irawati shouted, "Don't!" and hit him before he moved. Both sat on the floor sobbing, each sure the other was the bad one.

qa.q: What did Jeevan take on Wednesday?
qa.a: He took Irawati's crayon.

qa.q: Why did Irawati hit Jeevan on Saturday before he moved?
qa.a: She felt wronged and on guard after days of fights, so she expected him to spoil her tower and struck first.

qa.q: What could Amma do to stop the 'who started' loop?
qa.a: Separate them calmly, let each child say what happened, and name each one's feeling instead of hunting for who hit first.

qa.q: How does Jeevan see these fights?
qa.a: Jeevan feels wronged too, sure that Irawati is the bad one, since he gets hit and blamed.

grounding: Shows siblings retaliating until each fight is only about who hit first, both feeling wronged and unable to see the other's side.

subtype: Stage 4: Parent takes sides by accident [Observer]
passage:
"Ammi! Afreen pushed me!" Zayan wailed from the balcony.
Their Ammi, Rukhsana, rushed out and scooped him up. "Afreen! You're older, you should be sensible. How many times?"
"But he tore my drawing first..."
"Enough. Say sorry to your brother."
Afreen's chin shook. "Sorry," she mumbled, and ran to her room.
Sunaina Aunty, visiting from next door with ladoos, had seen it all. Softly she said, "Rukhsana, the drawing really was torn. I saw."
Rukhsana paused, Zayan on her hip. "Oh. I only heard him crying."
From the bedroom came Afreen's voice, small and loud at once: "You always take his side!"

qa.q: What had Zayan done to Afreen's drawing?
qa.a: He tore Afreen's drawing first.

qa.q: What does Sunaina Aunty's soft comment suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seemed concerned and a little uncomfortable, sensing that Afreen had been blamed unfairly.

qa.q: How could Rukhsana handle the next fight differently?
qa.a: She could pause, calm both children and ask each what happened before scolding, instead of siding with whoever is crying.

qa.q: What is it like for Afreen to hear 'You're older, you should be sensible' again?
qa.a: Afreen feels blamed and hurt, as if being older means being loved less, and bursts out that Ammi always takes his side.

grounding: Shows a parent rushing to the crying younger child and scolding the older one, who feels blamed again, as noticed by a visiting neighbour.

subtype: Stage 5: Separate, calm, listen to both [Response]
passage:
Monday. Eshaan and Mehak fought over the tower. Papa shouted, "Stop it, both of you!" Both cried louder.
Thursday. They fought again. This time Papa knelt down between them. "One at a time. Eshaan?"
"She knocked my tower!"
"You wanted your tower to stay up." Eshaan nodded, sniffing.
"Mehak?"
"He pushed me."
"You felt scared when he pushed." Mehak hiccupped and leaned on Papa.
The next Monday. A shout came from the rug. Before Papa got there, Eshaan said, "Papa, I'm angry, she took my block!" Mehak said, "I wanted a turn." Papa sat down with them, and the fight was over in a minute.

qa.q: What did Papa say to Eshaan on Thursday?
qa.a: He said, "You wanted your tower to stay up."

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when Papa said, 'You felt scared when he pushed'?
qa.a: She felt comforted and understood, so she hiccupped and leaned on Papa instead of crying louder.

qa.q: What did Papa change between Monday and Thursday that worked?
qa.a: Instead of shouting, he knelt at their level, let each speak in turn and named their feelings, which cooled the fight quickly.

qa.q: How might Eshaan experience being listened to?
qa.a: Eshaan feels heard, and by the next Monday he can say 'I'm angry' himself instead of only fighting.

grounding: Shows a parent getting down to the children's level, letting each tell their side and naming feelings, and how being heard cools fights.

subtype: Stage 6: One-on-one time and joint tasks [Response]
passage: From my balcony upstairs, I, Deepika, can see the Qureshi family's courtyard. Last spring Afreen and her little brother Danish fought all day over the swing. Lately something's different, though I can't know what they feel. Every evening at six, their mother sits alone with Afreen and a book. At half past six it's Danish's turn, with the ball. On Sundays their father brings cardboard boxes, and the two build a rocket together, arguing a little, then laughing. Yesterday Afreen held the tape while Danish stuck on windows. I heard her say, "Good job, rocket-man."

qa.q: When does the mother sit alone with Afreen?
qa.a: Every evening at six, with a book.

qa.q: What does Deepika seem to feel watching the courtyard now?
qa.a: Deepika seems pleased and a little touched by the change, while admitting not knowing what the children feel.

qa.q: Which two things seem to have eased the fights?
qa.a: A short daily time alone with a parent for each child, and a shared task like building the cardboard rocket together.

qa.q: How might Danish feel when Afreen says 'Good job, rocket-man'?
qa.a: Danish probably feels proud and happy to be praised by his sister while they build together.

grounding: Shows siblings whose rivalry eases with short daily one-on-one time with a parent and a shared building project, as seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Saturday
Usha Mami and everyone came for lunch today. The whole time it was Vikram this and Vikram that. My brother Vikram got 98 in maths. Vikram is going to be a doctor. Nani even gave him a hundred rupees. When Usha Mami asked about me, Amma said, "Manjula is good at drawing," and everyone said, "Oh, nice," and went back to Vikram. I went and sat on the stairs. I love Vikram, he helps me with fractions, but today I kind of hated him too. Maybe they love him more because he's clever. I got 71 in maths. Nobody gave me anything. I'm ten and I think I'm the less good one in this house.
Manjula

qa.q: How much did Vikram get in maths?
qa.a: Vikram got 98 in maths.

qa.q: Why did Manjula go and sit on the stairs?
qa.a: Manjula felt hurt and jealous, left out while everyone praised Vikram, and began to fear being the less loved one.

qa.q: What could Amma do to ease this comparison?
qa.a: Amma could notice Manjula on the stairs, spend time looking at Manjula's drawings, and praise each child's own efforts instead of letting marks decide.

qa.q: How might Vikram feel if he read this diary?
qa.a: Vikram might feel sad and surprised, since he helps with fractions and probably never wanted to be a rival.

grounding: Shows a ten-year-old hearing relatives praise a brother's marks and starting to feel like the less loved child.

passage: Last year my sister Maryam and I kept a secret list on the back of the kitchen calendar. Who got the bigger piece of cake. Who sat in front. Who went to bed later. I even measured our milk glasses with a ruler. When Maryam got a phone for Class 7, I cried so much that Ammi couldn't talk to me. It wasn't really the phone. My friend Minakshi asked, "Zainab, would you even use it?" I said no. I just wanted to know I counted as much as Maryam. Then Ammi took me out alone for ice cream and said, "You'll never be the same as Maryam, and I'll never love you less." I tore up my half of the list after that.

qa.q: What did Zainab measure with a ruler?
qa.a: Their milk glasses.

qa.q: What was Zainab really feeling when Maryam got the phone?
qa.a: Zainab felt jealous and unsure of being loved as much; it was not really about the phone at all.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that helped?
qa.a: Ammi spent time alone with Zainab and said plainly that the two would never be the same but the love would never be less.

qa.q: How might Maryam have felt about the secret list?
qa.a: Maryam may have felt watched and tired of every piece of cake being counted, and caught up in the same contest.

grounding: Shows a child keeping exact score of shares and treats with a sibling, when the real need is to know of mattering just as much.
